newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel says capital imports will continue.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel says capital imports will continue.

text.p: The big inflows of foreign currency into Israel that have exerted upward pressure on the shekel will continue even if interest rates fall significantly, a Bank of Israel report released on Thursday said.
It said the dollar inflow, which began in 1995, was caused by increased investor confidence in Israel's geopolitical situation and in the Bank of Israel's determination to fight inflation.

"These factors are expected to continue to be operative in the future, it appears without any connection to interest rate policy, because they arise from long-term considerations unrelated to short-term (interest) yields," the bank said.

Private sector capital imports grew to $6.4 billion in 1995 from $1.4 billion in 1994 and only fell moderately last year to $6.1 billion. Net investment in Israel by foreigners grew steadily in the period to $2.4 billion in 1996 from $1 billion in 1994.

The central bank has been criticised by the Treasury and many business leaders for its restrictive monetary policy and consequent high interest rates. High rates, in turn, have prevented the shekel from depreciating in line with Israel's inflation.
The shekel is therefore seen as overvalued, which has contributed to the current slowdown in the economy.
The Bank of Israel report categorically denied that lowering rates would improve the exchange rate situation.
"The key to returning to balance in the markets requires a return to fiscal discipline by the government," the report said, adding that the outlook was not good.
"In a situation similar to the last months of 1996, figures on the government deficit for January and the projected figures for February are not encouraging," it said.

The Treasury said the budget deficit reached an unexpectedly high 1.28 billion shekels in January, just one month into the fiscal year, but said it was due mainly to one-time factors. Finance Minister Dan Meridor has said the Treasury will review the budget after the first quarter, a decision the central bank in its report today criticised.
